study.title: Study of Luke 4: the Messiah tempted, rejected and acting with authority
study.overview: Luke 4 shows Jesus starting his ministry on two inseparable fronts: fidelity to the Father in temptation and public performance in the power of the Spirit. First, he faces the devil in the desert without giving in to the search for religious relief, power or display (vv. 1-13). Then, in Nazareth, Jesus declares that Isaiah's promise is being fulfilled in him, but the reaction of his city reveals rejection and unbelief (vv. 14-30). In Capernaum, his word is confirmed with authority over demons, fever and illness, and his mission is defined as a proclamation of the kingdom of God (vv. 31-44).

outline.title: Jesus is tempted in the desert and wins by the Word
outline.explanation: Full of the Holy Spirit, Jesus is led into the wilderness and spends forty days in trial. The devil tries to turn him from obedience to the Father by offering immediate satisfaction, political domination and religious display. In all the answers, Jesus submits to the Scriptures and refuses both autonomy and manipulation of God. The outcome is the temporary withdrawal of the tempter.

outline.title: The message of grace in Nazareth and the rejection of the listeners
outline.explanation: Back to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, Jesus teaches with fame and honor. In Nazareth, he reads Isaiah and applies the prophecy to himself, stating that the time of fulfillment has come. The initial reaction is of admiration, but soon it becomes resistance, because he confronts local expectations and recalls that the grace of God has also reached foreigners in the days of Elijah and Elisha. The murder attempt shows the hardness of the heart of the city.

outline.title: Authority of Jesus in Capernaum
outline.explanation: In Capernaum, his word impresses because it is not only informative, but powerful. He casts out a demon, and the unclean spirit recognizes his identity, although Jesus silences that testimony. He then heals Simon's mother-in-law and many other sick people, showing concrete compassion and domination over spiritual illnesses and forces.

outline.title: The mission of preaching the kingdom in other cities
outline.explanation: Even sought after by the crowds, Jesus does not allow himself to arrest himself for a single region or for expectations of permanence. He claims that he must proclaim the gospel of the kingdom of God to other cities, for he has been sent for this. The chapter ends with him preaching in the synagogues of Galilee, summarizing his missionary priority.

study.context: The chapter places the beginning of Jesus" public ministry after baptism and the divine affirmation of his sonship. Luke repeatedly highlights the action of the Holy Spirit, showing that the ministry of Jesus is not born of personal ambition, but from God's initiative. The setting includes the desert, Nazareth, Capernaum and other synagogues of Galilee. The notes provided suggest that Jesus begins his Galilean ministry in a region away from Jerusalem, which is presented as part of his humiliation. It is also mentioned that he starts acting more concentratedly in Capernaum.
study.theology: Luke 4 presents at least four central theological emphases. First, Jesus is the obedient Son who wins where Israel failed and where Adam fell: he resists the accuser without using his sonship for his own benefit. Second, true life comes from the word of God, and worship belongs only to the Lord; thus, the temptation to transform legitimate needs into sinful shortcuts is rejected. Third, Scripture is fulfilled in Jesus in a messianic and pastoral way: good news for the poor, liberation from the captives, restoration to the oppressed and the proclamation of the Lord's favorable year. Fourth, the authority of Jesus appears in word, teaching, exorcism and healing, but his mission is not only to settle immediate needs; he is sent to proclaim the kingdom of God. The rejection in Nazareth shows that the grace of God can offend when confronting pride, exclusivism or nationalist expectations. References to Elijah and Elisha indicate that divine mercy goes beyond borders of ethnic or local belonging. For an evangelical reading, this reinforces that the gospel calls faith, repentance, and submission to the lordship of Christ.

scholarViews.insight: The temptation in the desert shows Jesus resisting the devil and not taking shortcuts to power and glory; the parallel with Israel in the wilderness highlights that Jesus overcomes where the people failed.
Isaiah's reading in Nazareth is presented as the beginning of Christ's public ministry and as a statement that the prophetic promise is fulfilled in him.
Jesus declares that he must preach the kingdom of God to other cities; the miracles confirm his authority, but do not replace the priority of preaching.

questions: In which areas am I tempted to seek shortcuts, using legitimate needs as an excuse to disobey God?
Does my reaction to the Word of God look more like a passing admiration or obedient faith and repentance?
Have I valued the signs of Jesus" power more than his main mission to proclaim the kingdom of God?
study.practice: This passage calls the disciple to three concrete attitudes: feeding on the Word rather than living on impulses; humbly receiving the message of Jesus even when it contradicts personal expectations; and participating in the mission of the kingdom by giving priority to the gospel, without reducing Christ to a mere solver of problems. In practice, this can mean separating daily time for biblical reading and prayer, examining preferences that resist the correction of the Lord and serving the church and others with compassion, without losing focus on the proclamation of the gospel.
study.uncertainty: The given notes indicate that the order of temptations in Luke may not coincide with that of Matthew, but do not authorize the exact historical sequence. There is also Tyndale's observation of the use of 'Jew' in a broad sense in 4:44, but this is only an interpretative hypothesis based on the writing of the text. There is no safe data in the notes to define additional historical details about the sermon in Nazareth beyond what the chapter itself informs.
